claims.text: Mini-SWE-Agent's minimal linear loop achieves reported SWE-Bench Verified results in the same range as OpenHands's event-sourced conversation engine, despite OpenHands committing substantially more code to loop orchestration alone.

Mini-SWE-Agent's minimal scaffold reportedly achieves 74%+ on SWE-Bench Verified, while Codex's far larger codebase reports 69.1%; the figures are not directly comparable because the models, evaluation runs and deployments differ (Mini-SWE-Agent is unsandboxed, Codex is sandboxed).

A source-code study of eleven coding-agent systems found that loop sophistication does not predict benchmark performance; most code in production systems addresses safety, user experience, extensibility, clients and transport rather than task completion.

OpenHands reports ~66% on SWE-Bench Verified with Sonnet 4.5 and ~77% (77.6% in the at-a-glance table) with Opus 4.5 using its internal harness, the best of any open scaffold; SWE-agent's best Verified score with Opus 4.5 is listed as 72.0%.

SWE-agent's tool set is ls, find_file, open, scroll, edit, submit with a line-range linear edit format and full trajectory kept in context, whereas OpenHands offers bash, file_edit, browse, jupyter and custom MCP tools with str_replace plus full-file rewrite edits and event-history memory with a condenser.
The mini-SWE-agent, a 100-line-of-code descendant of SWE-agent, is often used for apples-to-apples model comparison.

SWE-agent's ACI is built on the hypothesis that standard Unix shells are poorly suited to language models: raw bash gives verbose error output, lacks guardrails against destructive file overwrites, and requires complex sed/awk invocations that trigger hallucinations.

SWE-agent's ACI provides open_file with a 100-line viewing window, scroll_up/scroll_down, regex-backed search_dir and search_file, and an edit command with automatic syntax validation and linter checks.
OpenHands builds on the CodeAct paradigm, in which the model emits executable Python and bash directly rather than rigid JSON tool-calling schemas.

OpenHands runtime uses an append-only event stream of Actions (CmdRunAction, IPythonRunCellAction, BrowseURLAction) and Observations (CmdOutputObservation, BrowserOutputObservation) passing through a central controller, enabling a planning agent to delegate subtasks to micro-agents.
OpenHands executes all actions inside isolated Docker containers or ephemeral cloud VMs, allowing arbitrary shell execution, dependency installation and headless browsing without risking the host.

OpenHands implements a 'runtime' that executes all agent actions in a Docker environment; the agent sends actions and receives observations, so it can run arbitrary code like a human developer without damaging the host machine.
SWE-agent uses configurable agent-computer interfaces to interact with isolated computer environments and employs SWE-ReX for sandboxed code execution.

OpenHands supports multi-agent coordination via AgentDelegateAction, where sub-tasks are delegated to specialized agents and results returned to the parent, and runs agents in per-session Docker containers.
In OpenHands' SWE-Bench Lite evaluation of 10 models (run on a cloud sandbox giving 30x or greater speedup), Claude 3.5 Sonnet was best with a 27% resolve rate using the default agent.

In the same OpenHands evaluation, o1-mini scored worse than GPT-4o, apparently because it 'overthought' and performed extra environment configuration instead of finishing the task; Llama 3.1 405B and deepseek-v2.5 were the strongest open models and beat some closed ones.

On SWE-Bench Lite (300 instances, no hints), OpenHands CodeActAgent v1.8 scored 26.0% with claude-3-5-sonnet at $1.10 average cost, 22.0% with gpt-4o at $1.72, and 7.0% with gpt-4o-mini, versus SWE-agent 18.0% with gpt-4-1106-preview and Aider 26.3%.

SWE-bench evaluates agents by running the agent-modified repository against a test suite including new tests from the human fix; the OpenHands paper reports all results without hint text and defaults to the SWE-bench Lite subset for cost saving.
SWE-bench Verified is a 500-issue subset in which OpenAI hired software engineers to filter out issues that were flawed or not solvable with the provided information.
AIDE reached 62.2% on SWE-bench Verified by scaling test-time inference with multiple complete runs and reward-based selection, at around $20 per issue.

Autonomous resolution of a complex multi-file bug on OpenHands or SWE-agent often consumes 300,000 to 2,000,000 tokens and 5 to 25 minutes per issue, while interactive tools like Aider and Cline use roughly 20,000 to 150,000 tokens per task.

OpenHands limitations reported include needing strong tests and well-scoped issues, high token cost on complex work, and security/ops concerns from its Docker-based runtime and Docker socket mounting.

OpenHands launched as OpenDevin in March 2024 as an open alternative to Cognition's Devin, is MIT licensed, and All Hands AI raised a $5 million seed round announced 5 September 2024 led by Menlo Ventures.
OpenHands announced state-of-the-art SWE-bench Verified results on 17 April 2025 using inference-time scaling and a critic model.

Sourcegraph's Amp does not expose model selection to users, which lets it switch backend models without user friction, and it uses 'handoff' (starting a new thread with needed context) rather than 'compact' summarization for context management.
